questions.prompt: What does traditional software operations assume that doesn't reliably hold for machine learning systems?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: That the same code, run the same way, produces correct behavior indefinitely, with no need to reassess correctness after launch

Traditional software assumes correctness verified once (via tests) stays valid until the code changes — ML breaks this because production data can drift, making a previously-correct model wrong with no code changes at all.
keyPoints: Traditional software assumes correctness verified once (via tests) stays valid until the code changes — ML breaks this because production data can drift, making a previously-correct model wrong with no code changes at all.

questions.prompt: What core disciplines do MLOps and LLMOps share, according to this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Versioning, a registry tracking deployed models, monitoring for degradation, and a plan for rollback or retraining

The fundamental lifecycle and operational discipline — versioning, registries, monitoring, rollback/retraining plans — applies to both classical ML and LLM-based systems.
keyPoints: The fundamental lifecycle and operational discipline — versioning, registries, monitoring, rollback/retraining plans — applies to both classical ML and LLM-based systems.

questions.prompt: What does schema validation check for in an ML data pipeline?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: That incoming data matches the expected structure — correct columns, types, value ranges, and no unexpectedly missing required fields

Schema validation catches structural data problems (format changes, unexpected nulls) before they can silently corrupt a training run or the resulting model.
keyPoints: Schema validation catches structural data problems (format changes, unexpected nulls) before they can silently corrupt a training run or the resulting model.

questions.prompt: What does a training pipeline orchestrator manage that a single manually-run script doesn't?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Multiple dependent steps (data fetch, validation, feature computation, training, evaluation, registration) as a defined pipeline with explicit dependencies, retries, and scheduling

An orchestrator manages the full multi-step process reliably, handling dependencies, retries, and scheduling that manual execution would leave to error-prone human coordination.
keyPoints: An orchestrator manages the full multi-step process reliably, handling dependencies, retries, and scheduling that manual execution would leave to error-prone human coordination.

questions.prompt: What does a model registry entry typically include?
questions.referenceAnswer: A registry entry ties together provenance (which run produced it), evaluation results, and lifecycle status, making a model version's full record queryable and authoritative.
keyPoints: A registry entry ties together provenance (which run produced it), evaluation results, and lifecycle status, making a model version's full record queryable and authoritative.

choices.text: Only the model's file name with no other detail
Which training run produced it, its evaluation metrics, its lifecycle stage, and the model artifact itself or a pointer to it
The personal notes of whoever trained the model
Nothing related to evaluation or provenance

questions.prompt: What does ML-specific CI/CD add on top of standard software CI/CD practices?
questions.referenceAnswer: ML CI/CD extends standard code-focused CI/CD with data validation gates, evaluation-threshold-gated model promotion, and automated deployment strategies specific to ML systems.
keyPoints: ML CI/CD extends standard code-focused CI/CD with data validation gates, evaluation-threshold-gated model promotion, and automated deployment strategies specific to ML systems.

choices.text: Nothing — ML CI/CD is identical to standard software CI/CD
Data validation as an automated gate, automated retraining/evaluation with a promotion threshold, and automated deployment via strategies like canary or shadow
Only the removal of any code review process
A requirement that deployment always happens manually

questions.prompt: What do operational metrics for a production ML system monitor?
questions.referenceAnswer: Operational metrics apply standard infrastructure monitoring practices to the model-serving component, covering the same kind of system health signals used for any production service.
keyPoints: Operational metrics apply standard infrastructure monitoring practices to the model-serving component, covering the same kind of system health signals used for any production service.

choices.text: Only the model's training accuracy from months ago
Latency, throughput, error rates, and resource utilization for the serving system, using standard software operational monitoring practices
The exact hyperparameters used during training
The personal satisfaction of the development team

questions.prompt: What does model governance add on top of the technical infrastructure (registries, lineage, experiment tracking) covered earlier in this course?
questions.referenceAnswer: Governance is the process layer that connects the technical record-keeping infrastructure to actual organizational decision-making and accountability.
keyPoints: Governance is the process layer that connects the technical record-keeping infrastructure to actual organizational decision-making and accountability.

choices.text: Nothing — governance is identical to the technical infrastructure itself
The human and organizational process — who approves deployment, what evidence is reviewed, how decisions get recorded — tying technical infrastructure to actual accountability
A replacement for data versioning and lineage tracking
Governance only applies to models that have already failed in production

questions.prompt: An offline experiment cannot be reproduced in deployment. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Version data, features, code and model artifacts. Record environment and preprocessing configuration. Reproduce a known input end to end before replacing the model.
keyPoints: Version data, features, code and model artifacts.
Record environment and preprocessing configuration.
Reproduce a known input end to end before replacing the model.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Reproduce a known input end to end before replacing the model. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Reproduce a known input end to end before replacing the model.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Version data, features, code and model artifacts. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Version data, features, code and model artifacts.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
